0.name: block
0.value:
Averages the values of an array: adds them up and divides by how many there are.

The mean is the everyday "typical value", the balance point of the data. Reach for it to smooth a set of readings into one number, to find the centre of a cloud of points, or to average each sensor over a window of frames. It uses every value equally - which is its strength, and its weakness: one wild value pulls it a long way (see THE OUTLIER below).

THE axis MENU:
With no axis (the default) the whole array is reduced to one number. With axis 0 the reduction runs DOWN each column, giving one result per column; with axis 1 it runs ALONG each row, giving one result per row. For a table of 5 frames (rows) of 4 sensors (columns), axis 0 answers "what did each sensor read on average", axis 1 "what did all the sensors read on average at each frame". The axis named is the one that disappears: a 5 by 4 array gives 4 values on axis 0, 5 on axis 1.

SYNTAX:
np.mean <axis: int>
With no argument there is no axis: the whole array becomes one number.

EXAMPLE:
np.mean 0

INPUTS and PARAMETERS:

in:
The array (a list or a single number is turned into one). Every array that arrives is averaged and the result sent - this is the only inlet that makes the node send.

axis (menu, also an inlet):
Which way to reduce - see THE axis MENU. Changing it does NOT send by itself; the next array uses it. The menu offers None (the whole array) and the axes the last array had (None and 0 for a 1-D array); a message None into the axis inlet also returns to the whole array. An axis the array does not have is treated as its last axis for that array only: the choice is kept, so one 1-D array through np.mean 1 does not stop the 2-D arrays that follow from being averaged along axis 1.

OUTPUTS:

mean:
With no axis, one number. With an axis, an array one dimension smaller:
a 6 by 8 array gives 8 means on axis 0, 6 on axis 1. Whole numbers still give a fractional mean.

THE OUTLIER:
The page opens with a glitch: load_bang switches the toggle on, and make_glitch puts a 30 into the cell at row 2, column 3 (third row down, fourth column across) - ten times the largest real value. At the top right np.mean and np.median each summarise all 48 cells. The mean jumps by more than half a step: 27 extra spread over 48 cells. The median, the middle value once sorted, barely moves - one value moving to the end of the line hardly changes what is in the middle. Click the toggle off and the two settle back together.

READING THE DEMO:
np.rand makes 6 rows by 8 columns of whole numbers 0 to 3, written in the cells; click its button for new ones. np.mean 1 averages along each ROW: the 6 means stand in the column to the right, each beside its row (np.expand_dims only turns them into a column). np.mean 0 averages down each COLUMN: the 8 means in the strip underneath, each under its column. The row and the column that run through the glitch are pulled far above the others - the colour scale stops at 3, so they show at its top - while every other mean is untouched.

RELATED:
np.median is the outlier-proof middle value. np.robust_mean averages only the values near the median. np.nanmean skips missing (nan) values, which make np.mean give nan. np.sum is the total before dividing. np.std measures how far values sit from the mean. t.mean is the PyTorch version.
